Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The tickets were for the 8:40 coastal train from North Quay to Bellhaven, and the return train was listed for 6:15 that evening. I had bought them together online in April and printed the confirmation at home because the station app had signed me out twice. The paper showed one booking code and two passenger names, but the tickets themselves had separate seat numbers. I brought the printout and both tickets in a blue folder, along with my bank card and the small receipt from the machine in the station hall.

The exchange counter is beside the information desk under the old clock, and there were four people waiting when I arrived at about ten past nine. A family was asking about a bicycle reservation, and a man in a green coat was trying to find a platform map. The queue moved slowly because one of the two windows was closed. A sign said that ticket returns and changes were handled at window three, and that online bookings needed the original ticket or a printed copy of the booking confirmation. I had both, so I stayed in line rather than calling the customer service number on the sign. The station was noisy from luggage wheels and an announcement about a signal check on the eastern line.

When I reached the counter, I said that I was returning both tickets because we could no longer make the trip. The clerk asked whether the booking included any hotel or ferry add-ons, and I said no, it was only the train journey. She looked at the two passenger names and checked that the seat numbers matched the booking. She asked to see the card used for payment, but I had paid with a different card from the one I brought, so she told me to keep the card ready in case the payment record needed checking. I explained that I had paid through the website with my sister's account, and she said the booking code would let her locate the transaction.

Numbered section:
1. The clerk scanned the booking confirmation first and then scanned each paper ticket separately. The scanner made a short tone for the first ticket and a longer tone for the second. She turned the screen slightly and asked me to confirm that both passengers were returning, and I said yes, both of us.
2. She said the return conditions were printed on the back of the receipt and pointed to the line about the five-pound handling charge. I asked whether the charge applied once to the booking or once to each ticket. She said it was one charge for the booking, not one charge per passenger.
3. She asked whether either ticket had been used or whether we had boarded any part of the journey. I said neither ticket had been used, and we had not travelled on any part of the route. She typed for a moment and checked the date on the first train against the date on the return train.
4. She handed me a narrow form with spaces for the booking code, the reason for returning the tickets, and a contact email. She said the form would be attached to the original booking, so I wrote the code carefully and checked the two names before signing.

I wrote that a family schedule had changed and put my sister's email address in the contact box because the booking belonged to her online account. The clerk asked whether she could send any update to that address, and I said yes, my sister checks it during her lunch break. The clerk read the address back slowly, and I confirmed the spelling. She placed the form beside the receipt and entered the booking code again. The window had a small ledge for bags, and I put the blue folder there while she handled the papers rather than holding everything in my hands.

While she was checking the record, she told me the exchange desk could not confirm the payment route from the printed receipt alone, and that the account holder might need to answer a follow-up message. I said my sister was at work until three and would be able to read email later in the afternoon. The clerk said if the account holder replied before four that day, the desk could keep the same file open for the afternoon review; otherwise, the note would remain attached to the booking for the next business day. I repeated the time because I wanted to make sure I had heard it correctly, and she said yes, before four.

She gave me the receipt back and asked me to check the booking code one more time. The last two characters were a seven and a one, rather than a seven and an i, and I read them from the printed copy. She compared the code with the screen and set the two tickets side by side under the glass window. The passenger names were in the same order as on the form, and the train times were visible near the bottom of each ticket. She said the return file had been entered and that the email address was the one she had on the form. She did not give me a date for any payment update.

I put the receipt and the form copy into the front pocket of the blue folder and kept the printed booking confirmation behind them. The clerk reminded me to keep the original tickets until the desk sent a message because the serial numbers might be needed if the account holder contacted them. I asked whether the message would go to my sister's address, and she said that was the address written on the form. I walked away from window three at about quarter to ten and stood near the timetable board to call my sister. I told her the desk needed an email reply before four if she could manage it, and that the receipt was in my folder. The board showed the coastal train still scheduled for Monday morning, and I left the station with both paper tickets in the folder."}]
